# rules/secrets.toml
[[rules]]
id = "cloud-access-key"
description = "example rule: cloud access key id"
regex = '''AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'''
keywords = ["akia"]
entropy = 3.0

[[rules]]
id = "generic-high-entropy"
description = "any 20+ char token with high entropy"
regex = '''[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]{20,}'''
keywords = []
entropy = 4.0
cp_redact.interface: def redact(text: str, rules: list[Rule], budget_ms: int = 50) -> dict  # {text_redacted, redactions: [{rule_id, start, end}], content_dropped: bool}

pitfalls: Using the plain re module on untrusted chat text: one crafted line can hang the daemon for minutes; use a linear-time engine plus the time budget
Writing the matched text into the redaction record or a log: the record keeps positions and rule ids only, or the secret leaks into the log
Hex strings top out at 4.0 bits, so a global 4.0 threshold misses hex secrets; give hex rules their own lower threshold

pitfalls: Keeping the signing key on the same account that publishes the package: one stolen login ships malware to every laptop; keep keys separate
Comparing versions as strings: '1.10.0' sorts below '1.9.0'; compare numeric tuples
Replacing the running build before the new one verifies: a failed update leaves a laptop with no capture and no way to recover; keep the old build until the new one runs
Exact notarisation and Intune or Jamf settings were not verified in our research: check current vendor docs before the first rollout
